3995.tone: Theil (first-hand, 2005-2007 fieldwork): 'Koorete is not a stress or accent language. It has two distinctive word level tones, a rising tone and a falling tone' (minimal pairs ʔáaʃ'e 'curse' / ʔàaʃ'e 'scratch', k'áme 'speak angrily' / k'àme 'become evening', s'óome 'throw' / s'òome 'fast'); rising = pitch rising throughout the word with the last syllable low before pause, falling = slightly falling pitch throughout the word. Theil reports the earlier analyses he rejects: Hayward 1982 'an accentual language, with an accent realized as a heightened pitch'; Ford 1990 'loudness, rather than heightened pitch … is the principle exponent of stress', plus a rare contrastive 'downward gliding tone... which occurs only on stressed syllables'. Azeb Amha 2007 (EAE 3:429-430, the scan excerpt): 'a clear distinction between two tones: high and low, but the occurrence of the high tone in a word is restricted. Because of this, K. is regarded as a tone-accent language.' No accessible source states a position for the accent/H/stress.

4002.dq: Trans-Zab exhibits a shift of word stress from the penultimate to the ultimate syllable in the nominal system (with some exceptions, chiefly adverbs)
4002.dloc: Mutzafi 2008: p. 415, sec. 4 'Penultimate > ultimate stress'; transcription note p. 411 fn. 8; JKS = J. Koy Sanjaq, p. 409 fn. 1.
4002.prule: Word stress is conditioned by word class and morphological make-up: in the nominal system (nouns, adjectives) it falls on the final syllable (a Trans-Zab shift from the pan-NENA penultimate; exceptions chiefly adverbs), e.g. nāšá 'man', nawtá 'nit', ganāwá 'thief'. No verbal rule is stated for this dialect; the paper's transcription default is penultimate (fn. 8), and the JKS verb forms it prints are final-stressed when the word ends in the bare present base or in the 1pl. ending -éx (šaqə́l vs J.Zakho šāqəl; ʾabé, ʾalé, ʾamə́r, ʾaxə́l, ʾezə́l, hawə́l, hawé, kawé, yaʾə́l; našqéx) and penultimate when a further suffix follows (šaqəlwa, nšiqle, nešqāle, nešqile, našqexən) and in ʾame, i.e. verbal stress follows the morphological build of the form, not a syllable count. Kim 2008 (citing the grammar, Mutzafi 2004b: 55f.) summarizes the group as final syllable of nominal and verbal STEMS with variable retraction in certain categories (vocatives).

4006.tone: Four-way tone contrast on monosyllables (H, L, R=LH, F=HL; Table 5 minimal pairs /pi/ 'dust' H, /pa/ 'string bag' L, /paj/ 'arrow' R, /pi/ 'rain' F). Monomorphemic disyllabic roots show only 6 of the 16 possible combinations (Table 6, p.17: H-L /pEwEl/ 'frog', L-H /pawil/ 'collarbone', L-L /duwE/ 'dog', L-R /dakaj/ 'eye', R-H /duwE/ 'ground', R-L /babol/ 'sago grub'; no Fall on either syllable, L-L the only identical-tone sequence, H-R unobserved; the text says 'less than half the theoretically possible tone patterns (4 x 4)'); the authors suggest word-level tone melodies (H~RH, L~LL, R~LH/LR, F~HL/RL, or a new LHL melody) matching Skou, Puare, Leitre and Barupu, supported by yung 'bird' (F) surfacing low in compounds; 'Much more data is needed before this hypothesis can be confirmed.' (p. 26) — contrasted with the phrase level at p. 185: 'chacun des constituants comporte un accent de hauteur, sur la dernière syllabe des bases de têtes nominales, et sur la première syllabe du verbe.'
4008.dloc: §2.8.2 'Accent de mot et parties du discours', p. 26 of the proofs (header '26 GRAMMAIRE KRYZ'); restated §10.1 p. 141 and §10.1.1 p. 141, §10.1.4 p. 143, §10.2.1 p. 144, §10.6 p. 155, §13.1 p. 185; attributive participle loses accent §19.1.3 'Participes épithètes' p. 345 (header 'RELATIVES 345'), ex. 1953-1954; 'accent de mot' also §12 p. 254 (sentence runs onto p. 255); base-final noun accent and tonic/atonic case suffixes p. 31 and p. 32; plural absolutive/genitive/locative paradigm riximbí/riximbe/riximbéˤ at §3.3.5 'Formation des génitifs pluriels' p. 40 (header '40 GRAMMAIRE KRYZ').
4008.prule: Accent position is fixed by word class and morpheme identity, not by syllable count or weight: nouns carry the accent on the final syllable of the base (p. 26 'Les noms sont accentués sur la syllabe finale'; p. 185 'sur la dernière syllabe des bases de têtes nominales'), with most inflectional suffixes atonic and a listed set of suffixes tonic (plural absolutive -mí/-bí/-mbí and -ar; the genitive in -i of the nouns that take it; the locative -éˤ), so that the accent moves onto a tonic suffix and otherwise stays on the base; all dependent/nominalised verb forms (masdars, gerunds and converbs, substantivised participles; also the future = imperfective participle + copula, and the interrogative forms) are accented on the FINAL syllable; independent finite indicative verb forms (all except the future) and place adverbs on the INITIAL syllable. Attributive adjectives, attributive participles and genitives are proclitic (unaccented); a participle heading an absolutive phrase is tonic but 'perd son accent s'il est épithète' (§19.1.3 p. 345). Accent position distinguishes segmentally identical forms (yi-qr-íc 'to seize' masdar vs yí-qr-ic 'was seized' aorist; xhiyíc 'to become' vs xhíyic 'became'; b-ar-í vs b-ár-i).
4008.srule: None described for simple words: Authier 2009 gives one (pitch) accent per word and says each constituent carries one 'accent de hauteur' (§2.8.2 p. 26; §13.1 p. 185); no secondary or rhythmic accent is mentioned anywhere in the accent passages (pp. 26, 88, 141-144, 155, 185, 345 read). Two accents are reported only for the periphrastic negative future, which keeps the participle's accent and that of the independent negative copula (§10.6 p. 155; ex. 598 p. 159).

Comme les formes verbales indépendantes, les adverbes de lieu ont un accent initial, avec un allongement expressif de la première syllabe. La place de l’accent permet de repére…

4008.idn: Source describes the Alik-village dialect (Quba district, NE Azerbaijan) of the Kryz dialect continuum (Kryz, Djek, Alik-Khaput); independent verb forms 'diffèrent considérablement entre les trois dialectes' (p. 141), so the verb-accent statements are Alik usage.

Le futur est formé du participe imperfectif, qui reste accentué sur la finale, et de la copule (p. 143) ... [formes interrogatives] accentuées…
4008.tone: Authier describes the accent as 'mélodique, montant ou descendant' (p. 26) and as an 'accent de hauteur' (p. 185), says it 'mériterait plus de recherches', and explicitly denies lexical tone ('Il n’y a en tout cas pas de tons absolus'); unaccented syllables show no vowel reduction. Realisation is thus pitch, but placement is a categorical rule by word class, so the record is coded set by morphology rather than tone or pitch accent; a reviewer who codes by realisation could label it pitch-accent.

Tone is lexical (fourteen noun tone classes I-XIV, sec. 1.3.8 pp.30-34: 'In lexicon every noun is specified with regard to its particular tonal pattern'; adjectives 'not predictable unless tonal patterns of them are specified in lexicon', p.61) and grammatical (verb aspect marked by a suprasegmental L morpheme; 'Every simple verbal stem bears a lexical high toneme in indicative', p.30). On stress: no accent/stress heading anywhere in the phonology (1.2 segments/harmony/sandhi/syllable canon, pp.2-8; 1.3 tone, pp.9-34); 'stressed/unstressed vowels' appear only as the vowel-sandhi condition (pp.6, 57, 61; same wording Hieda 2010: 8 fn.5, 9 and Hieda 2011: 6, 'The vowel sandhi rule is applied to unstressed vowels only'); p.378: tone languages 'including Kumam... do not make use of stress to express information structure in most cases'. tn.quote: Kumam is a tone language, exhibiting a low tone, a high tone, a falling tone, a rising tone, a downstep high tone and a double downstep high tone, which contrast on a phonetic level. However, a low toneme and a high toneme are posited in underlying representations. ... Phonetically there are four level tones in Kumam. ... tone bearing units (hereafter, TBU) consist of syllables ... There are two contour tones, a falling and a rising tone. ... Two tonemes, a high toneme and a low toneme, are posited in underlying representations. This supposition results in six tones in surface representations

4020.dq: In Gumbaynggir words, the stress falls on [1] a long vowel ... (Phrase-level intonation is treated separately, printed p. 290: 'The interrogative sentence has a rising intonation on the last word'.)
4020.dloc: Section 2.3 STRESS, p. 268 (viewed again in Stage C); vowel-length distribution pp. 265-266; cluster cross-reference 2.2.2 [iii] p. 267; intonation remark p. 290.
4020.heavy: 'a long vowel' (V:), and failing that 'a syllable-final vowel plus semivowel cluster' (Vy/Vw, e.g. gamáy 'spear', gáwgan 'shield'). By the wording of rule [2] only a semivowel coda counts; Eades gives no example of a non-glide closed second syllable without a long vowel (ŋáliwan 'jewfish' and gálugun 'one' have their closed syllable in final position only), so the lightness of other CVC syllables follows from the rule's wording rather than from a contrasting example.
4020.dflt: The first vowel (initial syllable): ɲámi 'woman', ŋáliwan 'jewfish'; in words of three or more syllables one of the middle vowels may receive stress instead (gálugun ~ galúgun 'one'). Initial /Cuw/ /Ciy/ syllables tend to lose their vowel with the second syllable stressed ([bwá:r], [gyéŋari]).
4020.prule: Stress falls on the long vowel; if there is no long vowel, on the (first) syllable-final vowel + semivowel sequence (Vy/Vw); if neither, on the first vowel, except that in words of three or more syllables one of the middle vowels may be stressed instead. Since a word has at most one long vowel and long vowels occur only in the first or second syllable (Eades pp. 265-266), this amounts to initial stress unless the second syllable is heavy (mí:mi, ɲámi, gáwgan vs ŋalí:, ŋalú:ŋgir, gamáy). Eades states that positional restriction for long vowels only; the same restriction for Vy/Vw sequences is Goedemans 1998's second-hand statement.
4020.srule: Not mentioned in Eades 1979, §2.3 Stress (p. 268) or elsewhere in the phonology chapter (§2, pp. 261-270): every example word, including 3-4-syllable ŋáliwan, ŋalú:ŋgir and gálugun~galúgun, carries a single stress mark.
